title: How the OpenTelemetry Collector shapes your telemetry pipeline
excerpt: The OpenTelemetry Collector lets you receive, process, and export telemetry outside your application code.
body:
A coffee shop that takes orders online can generate traces, logs, and metrics for each purchase. The order-processing code emits telemetry, but the notification never reaches the customer because the data never makes it to a backend that can trigger the alert. The OpenTelemetry Collector sits between the application and the observability platform, handling receipt, transformation, and delivery of that data.

In this post you will see why a dedicated collector simplifies consistent processing, how its three component types cooperate, and what to look for when picking processors that add context or trim volume. By the end you will know a concrete step to tighten your telemetry pipeline.

## Why use a collector for consistent processing

When a single service sends data straight to a backend, every deployment must embed export settings, retry logic, and any enrichment rules. Multiply that across dozens of services in staging, production, and multiple clouds, and the operational burden explodes. The Collector moves those responsibilities out of the application code and into a single, versioned binary.

The source points out that expanding from one coffee-shop location to several services creates a need for “consistent metadata, filtering rules, and export configurations across all of them.” A collector provides a shared layer where those rules live, so you no longer have to duplicate them in each codebase. It also lets you change export destinations without rebuilding the services, because the Collector alone handles the final hop to the backend.

## How receivers, processors, and exporters work together

The Collector arranges work into pipelines, each composed of three component types.

*Receivers* are the entry points. The article mentions the OTLP receiver, which “accepts traces, metrics, and logs from the OpenTelemetry SDK and forwards them to the appropriate pipeline.” Other receivers can pull data from Prometheus scrapes, syslog, or proprietary protocols.

*Processors* sit after receivers. They can add attributes, batch data, limit memory use, or drop unwanted signals. The source gives a concrete scenario: a resource processor adds an “environment” attribute so engineers can tell whether a measurement came from staging or production.

A batch processor then groups telemetry before it leaves the Collector, and a memory limiter protects the process from overload. The order matters, filters that depend on newly added attributes must run after the resource processor that creates them.

*Exporters* are the final stage. They hand the transformed data to backends such as Jaeger (via OTLP), Prometheus (via a scrape endpoint or Remote Write), or a logging store like OpenSearch. Because exporters are separate components, you can route the same telemetry to multiple destinations by attaching several exporters to a single pipeline.

Putting the three together looks like this: the ordering system’s SDK sends OTLP data → the Collector’s OTLP receiver captures it → a resource processor tags it with “env=prod” → a batch processor groups the spans → an OTLP exporter ships the batch to Jaeger, while a Prometheus exporter exposes metrics for scraping.

## Choosing processors to enrich and filter data

Selecting the right processors depends on the signals you need to keep and the context you want to add.

1. Resource processor, adds static attributes such as service name, version, or environment. Use it when you have multiple deployments and need a reliable way to separate their data.
2. Batch processor, groups telemetry into larger payloads, reducing the number of outbound requests. Helpful when the backend imposes rate limits or when network overhead is a concern.
3. Memory limiter, caps the Collector’s RAM usage. Essential in high-traffic setups to avoid OOM crashes.
4. Filter processor, drops spans, metrics, or logs that match a rule. Ideal for cutting noisy health-check requests or internal debug logs that would otherwise flood the backend.
5. Attribute processor, modifies or adds custom attributes based on existing ones. Use it to inject request IDs or customer identifiers that the application did not emit.

The source stresses that “processor order matters.” For example, if a filter depends on an “environment” attribute, the resource processor that creates that attribute must run first. Conversely, placing a batch processor before a filter would waste bandwidth on data that will later be discarded.

When configuring pipelines, start with the minimal set needed for correctness, usually a receiver, a resource processor, and an exporter. Then add batching, limiting, or filtering as you observe load patterns or cost concerns.

## The takeaway

A collector centralizes receipt, transformation, and export of telemetry, letting you enforce consistent processing across services. Use the OTLP receiver to pull data from SDKs, then chain processors, resource, batch, limiter, filter, in an order that respects their dependencies. Finally, attach exporters that match your observability backends. This modular setup keeps your application code lean and gives you a single place to tweak how telemetry flows.
